name: Normal approximation
seoTitle: Normal approximation Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Normal approximation: work out probability of failure (0<q<1) from the probability of success and number of occurrences. A free statistics…
summary: The Normal approximation calculator turns the probability of success, number of occurrences and number of successes into probability of failure (0<q<1). That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Normal approximation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Normal approximation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports probability of failure (0<q<1) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the event restatement); then you type in the probability of success (0<p<1), number of occurrences (N) and number of successes (n).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Normal approximation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Probability of failure (0<q<1)=1 − probability of success (0<p<1)
Mean (μ)=number of occurrences (N) × probability of success (0<p<1)
Standard deviation (σ)=(the square root of ((number of occurrences (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × probability of failure (0<q<1))))
Variance (σ²)=(number of occurrences (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × probability of failure (0<q<1))
Z-score=(number of successes (n), mean (μ), (the square root of ((number of occurrences (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × probability of failure (0<q<1)))), event restatement)
Z-value=((number of successes (n), mean (μ), (the square root of ((number of occurrences (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × probability of failure (0<q<1)))), event restatement))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Probability of success (0<p<1) = 0.5, Number of occurrences (N) = 100, Number of successes (n) = 40 and Event restatement set to P(x ≥ n) — it reports Probability of failure (0<q<1) = 0.5, Mean (μ) = 50, Variance (σ²) = 25 and Standard deviation (σ) = 5.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Probability of failure (0<q<1) = 0.5, Mean (μ) = 50, Variance (σ²) = 25 and Standard deviation (σ) = 5 should be roughly the size you expected from Probability of success (0<p<1) = 0.5 and Number of occurrences (N) = 100.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Normal approximation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the probability of success, number of occurrences and number of successes — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Normal approximation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns probability of failure (0<q<1), derived from the probability of success, number of occurrences and number of successes. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Normal approximation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the probability of success, number of occurrences and number of successes, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Probability of failure (0<q<1) = 0.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Normal approximation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
